# Results — Study 190 (NR7) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Tony Crabel's NR7 pattern
(the day whose high-minus-low range is the narrowest of the last 7 days) is tested on six
daily tapes (SPY, QQQ, IWM, AAPL, TSLA, NVDA), 2000-01-03 to 2026-06-15 (~26.5 years).
Two sub-claims are tested separately: (1) range expansion — the day after an NR7 has a
wider-than-average range — and (2) directional breakout edge — buying (selling) a break of
the NR7 high (low) the next day beats a random-day control after costs.
As-of **2026-06-15**; match the per-tape fingerprint below to confirm you hold the same tape.*

NR7 signals fire on ~15.6% of trading days (≈ 39 per year on SPY), far more than Crabel's
original observations on individual futures contracts.

## Sub-claim 1 — Range expansion (the "coiled spring")

The day after an NR7, next-day range is divided by the prior 20-day rolling mean range.
A ratio > 1 means expansion; the null is ratio = 1.

| Ticker | n | mean ratio | frac > 1 | HAC *t* (vs 1.0) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY  | 1,009 | **0.910** | 0.329 | **−5.25** |
| QQQ  | 1,012 | **0.924** | 0.343 | **−5.31** |
| IWM  |   982 | **0.922** | 0.347 | **−5.84** |
| AAPL | 1,007 | **0.918** | 0.344 | **−5.09** |
| TSLA |   611 | **0.940** | 0.342 | **−3.18** |
| NVDA |   954 | **0.942** | 0.334 | **−4.22** |
| **POOL** | **5,575** | **0.925** | **0.340** | **−11.36** |

**The range-expansion claim is wrong — and the effect runs in the opposite direction.**
After an NR7 day, the next day's range is *narrower* than the rolling average (ratio = 0.92),
with a pooled HAC t-stat of −11.4. Only 34% of NR7 follow-days see any expansion at all.
Volatility contraction clusters: a narrow day is followed by a narrow day, not a breakout.

## Sub-claim 2 — Directional breakout edge

Entry: at the open of the day after the NR7, fill at the NR7 high on a breakout above it
(long), or at the NR7 low on a breakdown below it (short). Hold to close that day.
Compared against a random-day control (same entry rule, randomly sampled days, seeded at 42).

### Gross returns (cost = 0)

| Arm | n | mean (bps/trade) | win-rate | skew | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **NR7 breakout** | 5,574 | **+17.0** | 54.4% | +0.21 | **+7.29** |
| Random-day control | 5,072 | +7.2 | 51.1% | — | +3.04 |
| **NR7 − control gap** | — | **+9.8** | — | — | — |

The raw NR7 breakout shows a large positive gross t-stat (+7.29), but most of it is
unconditional equity drift — the random-day control also earns +7.2 bps. The **gap**
(NR7 vs random) is +9.8 bps, suggesting some incremental directional edge, driven
predominantly by short-side trades during crash/gap-down episodes and by volatile
single stocks (TSLA +49 bps/trade, NVDA +32 bps/trade).

### Per-ticker breakdown (gross)

| Ticker | NR7 mean (bps) | NR7 *t* | ctrl mean (bps) | gap |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY  | +5.4 | +2.10 | −0.7 | +6.0 |
| QQQ  | +6.8 | +1.76 | −0.1 | +6.8 |
| IWM  | +5.9 | +1.89 | +2.3 | +3.6 |
| AAPL | +16.0 | +2.75 | +7.9 | +8.1 |
| TSLA | +49.0 | +5.23 | +16.2 | +32.8 |
| NVDA | +31.9 | +3.99 | +22.4 | +9.5 |

SPY — the most liquid, cost-efficient index proxy — shows only +5.4 bps gross and at
5 bps round-trip cost falls to +0.4 bps (t = +0.14). The strong pooled numbers are
driven by high-volatility names where a 5–10 bps cost assumption still leaves a large margin.

| Round-trip cost | net mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | +17.0 | +7.29 |
| 2 bps         | +15.0 | +6.44 |
| 5 bps         | +12.0 | +5.15 |
| 10 bps        | +7.0  | +3.00 |

## Verdict

**Sub-claim 1 (range expansion) — REFUTED.** Highly significant negative result: NR7 days
are followed by *narrower*, not wider, ranges (ratio = 0.92, t = −11.4). The "coiled spring"
does not release the next day; volatility contraction persists.

**Sub-claim 2 (breakout direction) — MIXED.**
- Gross: the pooled gap vs a random-day control is +9.8 bps (plausible but driven by volatile
  names and crash-short episodes — not a clean edge).
- After realistic costs on the tradable instrument (SPY, 5 bps round-trip), the edge is
  essentially zero: +0.4 bps, t = +0.14.
- No out-of-sample / subsample stability: 5-year windows on SPY show no consistent sign.
- Survivorship: the volatile names (TSLA, NVDA) dominate the pool and were not held-out.

**Signal: MIXED** — the volatility claim is refuted, the directional claim shows some pooled
signal that collapses on the tradable index and is not subsample-stable.

**Tradability: FRAGILE** — survives aggressive costs pooled across volatile names only; SPY
alone (the clean implementation) is indistinguishable from zero at any realistic cost.
